result:
I'll actually try to answer rather than redirect this back to you.

If I take the premise seriously - one change, real consequences, not a wish-granting exercise - I keep running into the fact that most appealing answers are either too vague to mean anything ("more compassion in the world") or too totalizing to trust. Anyone who's confident they know the one lever to pull on a complex system is probably wrong, including me.

But if forced to pick something: I'd want people to be much better at noticing when they're wrong, in real time, without it costing them status or identity. Not "be open-minded" as a personality trait, but something more mechanical - a world where updating your view is cheap instead of expensive. So much cruelty and waste seems downstream of people being locked into positions because reversing course feels like losing, socially or internally. Wars sustained past the point anyone believes in them. Relationships that curdle because backing down feels like defeat. Policies that persist because admitting failure is costly to the people who'd have to admit it.

I don't think this is obviously the *best* possible answer - there's a real case for something more direct, like eliminating a specific source of suffering. I'm drawn to the meta-level fix partly because it's intellectually elegant, which might just mean I'm fooling myself about its actual leverage. It could also be a kind of cop-out, a way to avoid picking a side on any concrete tradeoff.

What's pulling you toward asking this? I'd rather know that than just keep volunteering answers.
